accroche: Ten poems published in her lifetime, without her name. Her editors smoothed her punctuation sixty-five years before anyone read it as she wrote it.
contenu_vulgarise:
When Emily Dickinson dies in 1886, in Amherst, she has seen only ten of her poems in print, all of them published without her authorization and without her name, slipped anonymously into newspapers between 1850 and 1878. Her sister Lavinia, tidying her room, discovers something else: about 1,800 poems, more than eight hundred of them carefully copied into some forty small notebooks sewn by hand, the rest on loose sheets and unbound booklets. Faced with this discovery, Lavinia says she feels a sort of “Joan of Arc vocation”: she decides on her own to have published what her sister had never shown to anyone.

## A Poetry Corrected Before It Is Published

Lavinia entrusts the notebooks to Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson, who publish *Poems* in 1890. The success is immediate: eleven reprintings in less than two years. But Todd and Higginson do not content themselves with copying the texts. They regularize the meter, correct the rhymes they judge imperfect, add titles to poems that had none, and, above all, remove almost all the dashes that punctuate Dickinson's writing, replacing them with more conventional commas or periods. A second series follows in 1891, then a third, edited by Todd alone, in 1896. A family dispute over a land division between the Dickinsons and the Todds then halts all serious editorial work for more than thirty years. For the first hundred fifteen poems published, it is these choices of 1890, not Dickinson's, that generations of readers take for her writing.

## What Sixty-Five Years of Smoothing Concealed

The dashes are nonetheless not hesitations of the pen. In Dickinson, they cut the line off the beat, suspend a sentence before its fall, leave a meaning open rather than closed. This choice is as deliberate as her punctuation is irregular. It takes until 1955, and the critical edition by the scholar Thomas H. Johnson, published by Harvard, for someone to return to the original manuscripts rather than to Todd and Higginson's transcriptions. Johnson restores the punctuation, the unusual capital letters, the chronological order of the poems. Sixty-five years after Dickinson's death, her readers finally discover lines that no one before them had read as she wrote them. Many of these poems nevertheless keep, even today, a title that Dickinson never wrote: the additions of 1890 blended so well into the legend of certain poems that they sometimes survive the correction that followed.

repere.texte: Ten of Emily Dickinson's poems appeared in her lifetime, all published without her authorization and without her name, between 1850 and 1878. Nearly 1,800 others were discovered only after her death, in 1886, by her sister Lavinia.
repere.source: Emily Dickinson Museum, “Publications in Dickinson's Lifetime”

carte.punch: Emily Dickinson's dashes were erased for sixty-five years before being restored.
carte.idee: Of nearly 1,800 poems found at her death, only ten had appeared in Emily Dickinson's lifetime. Her first editors then regularized her punctuation; it would take until 1955 to read her poems with their original dashes.

quiz.question: Why do the first printed editions of Emily Dickinson's poems not show exactly what she wrote?
choix: Because the first editors regularized her punctuation and dashes to make them more conventional
Because her sister Lavinia rewrote the poems from memory, the original manuscripts having been destroyed
Because Emily Dickinson herself asked for her poems to be published in a simplified form
Because the only poems found after her death were unfinished drafts
quiz.explication: The manuscripts were not destroyed: Lavinia found nearly 1,800 of them, more than eight hundred carefully copied into notebooks. Dickinson never asked for this simplification. She authorized none of her ten publications in her lifetime. It was Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson who, in 1890, regularized rhymes, meter, and punctuation; it would take Thomas H. Johnson's edition, in 1955, to restore the original text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many of Emily Dickinson's poems were published in her lifetime?
choix: About eight hundred, gathered in hand-sewn notebooks
None: all her poems were published after her death
Ten, all appearing without her authorization and without her name
Nearly eighteen hundred, in several regional newspapers
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that only ten poems appeared in Dickinson's lifetime, all published without her authorization and without her name, between 1850 and 1878.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Lavinia Dickinson feel on discovering her sister's poems after her death?
choix: Strong reluctance, which makes her want to destroy them
A sort of Joan of Arc vocation, which drives her to have them published
Indifference, before handing them at random to a printer
Anger at her sister for never having shown them
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On discovering the manuscripts, Lavinia says she feels a sort of Joan of Arc vocation, and decides on her own to have published what her sister had shown to no one.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How successful is the Poems edition published by Todd and Higginson in 1890?
choix: A single edition, quickly sold out and never reprinted
A commercial failure, remedied only after Todd's death
An immediate translation into several European languages
Eleven reprintings in less than two years
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that the 1890 edition's success is immediate: eleven reprintings in less than two years.
